key_insight: Disordered metal-oxide photonic glasses can produce target facade colors for building-integrated photovoltaics, but true angle-independent color is not achieved and the result depends strongly on oxide choice, encapsulant, and viewing geometry.
engineering_relevance: This work shows how to tune visually acceptable photovoltaic coatings without relying on absorptive pigments, while quantifying the tradeoff between color fidelity and optical performance on realistic module stacks.
method: Modeled scattering with Mie theory, Percus-Yevick structure factor, and exact phase functions.
Combined optical transport using two-flux transfer with absorption/refraction at the front glass.
Mapped color outcomes across oxides, encapsulants, cell technologies, particle sizes, packing fractions, and layer numbers.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that all four target colors were matched in a three-layer coating within DeltaE00 of 0.8 to 2.5, but day-to-day viewing changes caused DeltaE00 shifts of 5 to 18.
watch_item: The claimed disorder-based color is not fully angularly stable in real facade conditions, so oxide selection and facade geometry must be co-designed rather than assumed interchangeable.
paper_title: Engineering Color and Angular Stability in Building-Integrated Photovoltaics Using Metal-Oxide Photonic Glasses
